stories.title: How ShipStation Global built an AI IT help desk on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
stories.summary: ShipStation Global's engineering team built Deckhand, an AI IT help desk agent for Slack on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. It answers routine IT questions from a curated knowledge base, reads error-message screenshots, and files Jira tickets. In its first three months it resolved 97.5% of channel queries with a 96% positive feedback rating.

sources.title: How ShipStation Global built an AI IT help desk on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
sources.text: This post is co-written with Kenneth Salmon, Edward Boswell, Jack Armstrong, Robert Banh, and Nick Ciubotariu from ShipStation Global. Answering the same IT questions and clearing routine tickets drains time that IT teams could spend elsewhere. To reclaim it, the ShipStation Global Engineering team built Deckhand , an AI-powered IT help desk agent for Slack, on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore . ShipStation Global is the leading intelligent shipping and logistics platform for small and mid-sized shippers, and it operates on a simple belief: the more efficient its teams are, the better it delivers for customers. Deckhand puts that belief to work. It answers routine IT and company questions from a curated knowledge base, reads error-message screenshots, and creates and updates Jira Service Management tickets. In this post, we discuss how ShipStation architected Deckhand, which resulted in resolving 97.5 percent of incoming channel queries while earning a 96 percent positive feedback rating by employees (Figure 1). Figure 1: 3-month channel coverage and positive feedback The problem Deckhand solves is the one every IT team will recognize: the same questions are routinely asked, error messages are posted after business hours, and information needs to be gathered from different teams. At ShipStation Global, those conversations lived in a busy help desk Slack channel, where employees asked, and IT answered, one thread at a time. The answers usually already existed in a Confluence how-to article, on a company intranet page, or in a thread from eight months earlier. Finding them was the hard part. The channel data made the scale concrete. In the 12 months before launch: “We created Deckhand because getting help should be as simple as asking a question in Slack, not deciphering a ticket form or sending an email into the void. We believe that tickets are an indication of operational friction not productivity. Deckhand resolves common questions on the spot and, when it can’t, converts the conversation into a fully contextualized ticket with one click, improving the employee experience and freeing our team from endlessly repeating the phrase: ‘Please file a ticket.’” — Chris Collins, Senior Director IT at ShipStation Global Deckhand works in Slack like any teammate—joining channels, reading the conversation, and drawing context from Slack profiles to answer IT questions in place. We run it on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, hosts the agent in isolated sessions, so we run no servers or containers. The solution has four main components, shown in Figure 2: Figure 2: Architecture diagram showing Slack events entering the Slack service and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, with separate paths to an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base, AgentCore Gateway-backed Lambda tools, Jira Service Management, and DynamoDB feedback. When an employee posts in a channel where Deckhand is a member, the Slack service assembles the full thread history and user context. It then invokes the agent through the AgentCore runtime API. The agent searches the knowledge base and calls tools as needed. When it finds an answer, it returns a final response (Figure 3). When it doesn’t, it asks a clarifying question or offers to create a ticket (Figure 4). Figure 3: Deckhand responds with self-service steps Figure 4: Deckhand offers to create a ticket This section walks through how Deckhand is implemented, from prerequisites to a working deployment. To implement this pattern, you need the following: The agent is intentionally lightweight. Using the open source Strands Agents SDK , an agent consists of a model, a set of tools, and a system prompt. The SDK manages the reasoning loop, allowing the model to select tools, process results, and iterate until it produces an answer. Deckhand’s agent service is implemented in a few lines of Python. The model ID is set through an environment variable, which allows switching models without modifying application code. Tools are integrated with the agent in two ways. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases retrieval is a native Strands tool that supports knowledge base search with a single import. Other functions, including classification, ticket management, user resolution, and image analysis, are handled by a Lambda function registered on AgentCore Gateway. The Gateway exposes these as MCP tools, and the Lambda routes each invocation by tool name. This separation allows tool logic to be updated independently, and the agent can access new tools from the Gateway without requiring a rebuild. AgentCore runtime hosts the agent as a container, avoiding the need for server or session management. The Slack service calls the agent synchronously for each message, providing the thread transcript and user context, and posts the final response. Since context, including the employee’s profile, is included with every request, the agent can complete ticket details automatically. Deckhand answers from a single Amazon Bedrock knowledge base with core S3-backed data sources: Each document includes metadata such as title, source URL, content type, and event dates. This allows the agent to filter content, for example, when users ask about upcoming events or weekly lunch menus in the Austin office. The most valuable data source is the archive of resolved support threads. Before Deckhand existed, Slack was where problems got solved: years of employees describing issues and IT walking them through fixes. That history is an organic knowledge base, validated by the best possible reviewer: the person whose problem got fixed. It’s also noisy: a raw export mixes banter, automated alerts, and threads that never actually got resolved. sources.title: How Block is building AI-powered security with OpenAI technology
sources.text: Block is using AI systems including OpenAI Daybreak to compress the time to fix vulnerabilities, freeing its security team to focus on strategic work. Hour to replay a proposed detection change against seven months of telemetry Minutes from submitting a high-level vulnerability to an automated proposed patch Analyst-hours of investigation completed each quarter At Block, the company behind Square, Cash App, and Afterpay, the security team leverages the OpenAI Defense Factory: where AI handles vulnerability discovery, detection, and response at a scale that no human team could keep up with. With AI systems including OpenAI Daybreak, Block is taking just hours to do work that used to take weeks. Block’s security team has been focused on responsibly adopting AI across workflows, whether that’s code generation or security operations. “What it’s really centered on is having a new teammate that you can scale with,” James Nettesheim, Chief Information Security Officer, says. “It’s not like a more traditional automation where you had to go step by step. You can prompt it with a fairly bespoke, ambiguous problem and work through it together.” Projects like reviewing a software bug or parsing a log would take days or weeks to complete. Now the team can complete those projects in a fraction of the time, with a human still validating every result. For example, for detection tuning, every investigation stores its raw query evidence, so the team can now replay a proposed detection change against seven months of production telemetry in under an hour. That work used to mean requerying hundreds of old cases by hand, and often it rarely happened in practice since it was so time-consuming. The team has also gotten more particular about which model they’re using for which job. “We used to use the latest model, but you don’t need to do that anymore,” he says. “It’s been a learning experience to choose different models for different tasks.” Block’s security harness is built on top of Daybreak to help route tasks to the right model, and it includes hooks for humans to take over tasks or for agents to verify each other’s work. The team continually evaluates these systems against internal benchmarks and real-world performance, adjusting its approach when needed, including routing work to human review when that is the responsible path. The automated triage system has resulted in faster work (and more of it) getting done. Block’s security team has seen a 50% boost to triage throughput, a 50% increase in intelligence gathering and investigations, and an entirely new autonomous hunting capability. Nettesheim says, “This performs ~1,100 analyst-hours of investigation per quarter, because every alert now gets a full, deep investigation across all elements the alert involves. Our system works every alert like it’s the only alert we’ve got that day.” Traditional scanning tools flag a single vulnerability in isolation, but Block’s security team can go much further with Daybreak. The model helps hypothesize about attack patterns and chain together a series of attacks into a full end-to-end compromise path, surfacing vulnerabilities that might have existed for years. In one case, an alert on a single laptop looked like a minor policy issue on its own. But during peer review, the model followed an indicator that appeared only incidentally in the evidence, joined it against Block’s identity logs, and surfaced a much larger set of issues. “One routine endpoint alert became a campaign takedown. No single tool makes that join. The signal only exists across two products’ logs,” James says. Another example when Daybreak helped was during a recent red team exercise. The model was given a few hints about an internal system, and it chained together a full attack path—SQL injection, privilege escalation, a foothold, credential enumeration, and a pivot to other systems—in about two hours. This would typically take a human red teamer several days. In recent red team exercises, the time from submitting a high-level vulnerability to an automated proposed patch was 18 minutes. Finding the vulnerabilities is only as good as the ability to fix them. Nettesheim walks through the process his team uses on every finding: locate where the issue lives in the code and identify who owns it, then move to remediation. “You propose a patch, you confirm exploitability, and then you verify that you have fixed it, with a human in the loop guiding it and deploying the code changes.” While agents are technically capable, they don’t carry an organization’s context or the reasoning behind previous decisions. A human provides that context and strategy, and that’s where his team comes in to provide a human layer of review. As AI’s judgment is proven out in practice, Nettesheim says, “we’ll slowly ladder up the risk level to use it for more sensitive systems.” Less than one hour to replay a proposed detection change against seven months of telemetry. 18 minutes from submitting a high-level vulnerability to an automated proposed patch in recent red team exercises. Roughly 600 analyst-hours per quarter of false-positive triage handed back. Approximately 1,100 analyst-hours of investigation completed per quarter. 50% increase in intelligence gathering and investigations. Detection and response work alone has handed back roughly 600 analyst-hours per quarter that used to go toward triaging false positives. With that time back, the team now spends more time on deeper investigations and building more automation responsibly. As the pace of attack increases and AI models keep advancing, Nettesheim sees an opportunity to reduce the number of vulnerabilities introduced in the first place. sources.title: How Tamnoon built AI-powered cloud security remediation with Amazon Bedrock
sources.text: Critical cloud exposures pile up faster than security teams can close them. Cloud-native application protection platforms (CNAPP), cloud providers, and posture scanners generate more findings than any team can triage, and risk accumulates in the gap between detected and fixed. Most findings sit untouched, not because they’re hard to fix. Someone must investigate context, identify the owner, confirm the fix won’t break production, and then do it at a volume that outpaces headcount. In this post, we share how Tamnoon built Tami, an agentic cloud remediation orchestrator on Amazon Bedrock , to close that gap. Tami autonomously investigates findings ingested from CNAPP and cloud-native sources and assesses whether remediation is safe. It then generates and orchestrates the fix with guardrails and governance wherever a change touches a customer’s cloud. The approach drove an over 90 percent reduction in critical cloud exposure in 90 days with zero production issues. Tamnoon is an AI-powered cloud security remediation platform that works alongside CNAPPs. Its AI assistant, Tami, helps human cloud security experts investigate, prioritize, and safely remediate misconfigurations and issues across customer environments in AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and other cloud providers. Tamnoon integrates with the CNAPPs and cloud-native tools teams already use and turns their findings into validated, production-safe fixes. Most of the work including investigation, prioritization, and remediation planning happens before anything touches a live environment, which is what makes automated remediation trustworthy at scale. A security engineer can spend hours investigating a single finding. Often, it traces back to the same root cause as dozens of other alerts. Tamnoon’s solution addresses the full pipeline from finding ingestion to validated fix. The platform treats these challenges as interconnected rather than isolated problems. Tamnoon takes you from initial finding to executing the fix. The platform ingests findings from CNAPP, Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM) providers, and other security tools and normalizes them into a unified schema. It then enriches them with asset and exposure context and prioritizes them. From there, the agentic layer takes over using a set of specialized AI agents, each running in an event-driven, serverless architecture on AWS, so every stage scales independently and fails safely. The platform delegates work to four specialized agents, each responsible for a distinct phase of the remediation pipeline: When the Tamnoon team set out to build Tami, the choice of foundation model (FM) platform was going to shape everything that followed. Tamnoon’s remediation agents don’t all do the same kind of work. Some perform deep investigative reasoning to understand the root cause of a security finding. Others handle high-volume validation, checking proposed fixes quickly and cheaply. Still others review generated code, balancing quality against cost on every task. Matching each of these jobs to the right model, without stitching together a different integration for each one, was a core requirement. That requirement is what made Amazon Bedrock the natural fit. Through a single API, each agent can call the foundation model best suited to its task. The most capable models handle the hardest reasoning. More efficient models take on the repetitive, high-throughput work. Review-focused models optimize the trade-off between output quality and cost. Because it’s one integration rather than many, models can be swapped or upgraded as the landscape evolves, without re-plumbing the architecture each time. Operational overhead at scale was another factor in the decision. As request volume grew, Tamnoon wanted to avoid building and maintaining its own logic to distribute traffic across regional capacity. Amazon Bedrock Cross-Region inference handles this automatically. It automatically routes inference requests to the optimal AWS Region within a defined geographic boundary, maintaining throughput without requiring any custom routing code to operate. Security was the final consideration, and for a cloud security company it was non-negotiable. With Bedrock, inference runs inside Tamnoon’s own AWS environment under AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM)-scoped permissions. Sensitive customer data never leaves the trust boundary. That gave the team confidence that the platform underpinning Tami met the same standard Tamnoon holds its own service to. Tamnoon sits downstream of the detection tools security teams already run. CNAPPs like Wiz, CrowdStrike, Palo Alto Cortex, Upwind, SentinelOne, Orca, and Cyera along with cloud-native services like AWS Security Hub and Amazon GuardDuty are the source of truth for what’s wrong in the environment. Tamnoon connects through API-based integrations and normalizes findings into a common format, so a misconfiguration looks the same whether it came from Wiz or GuardDuty. The detection tools remain the foundation. Tamnoon delivers the end-to-end remediation that follows. For every finding it works, Tami assigns a Remediation Confidence Indicator (RCI) of SAFE, RISKY, or AWAITING DATA. That rating tells teams what can be automated and what needs human review first. Tamnoon runs entirely within its own AWS accounts, isolated per environment. Users access the platform through a single secure entry point built on Amazon API Gateway, with encryption managed by AWS Certificate Manager and sign-in handled by Amazon Cognito. Everything behind that entry point runs in private networks across multiple Availability Zones, so the core platform is never directly exposed to the internet. Inside that environment, Tamnoon combines two kinds of compute. Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) runs the always-on services behind the dashboard, while AWS Lambda powers the event-driven work of collecting findings, analyzing them, and executing remediations. stories.title: Now You Can Invite Anyone to a WhatsApp Call
stories.summary: You can now invite anyone to a WhatsApp call, even if they don’t have a Whatsapp account, so you can connect with people without worrying what apps they have. The post Now You Can Invite Anyone to a WhatsApp Call appeared first on Meta Newsroom .

sources.name: Meta Newsroom
sources.title: Now You Can Invite Anyone to a WhatsApp Call
sources.text: Today we’re making WhatsApp calling more open than ever. With guest calling, you can now invite anyone to join a WhatsApp call — even if they don’t have a WhatsApp account. That means free, end-to-end encrypted calls for everyone with no time limits, so there are no abrupt cutoffs, scrambling to restart the call, or waiting for everyone to rejoin. Anyone joining as a guest always needs the call host’s approval. Guests will enter a waiting room until the host lets them in and guests can be removed from the call at any time. Guests can’t see other participants’ phone numbers, send messages, or add anyone else directly to the call. To get started, navigate to the Calls tab in WhatsApp, select the “+” icon, create a call link, and send it to the people you want to talk to — colleagues, classmates, or tutor — without having to worry about what apps they have. Guests can open the link in their computer browser, type in their name, and join 1:1 and group calls with up to 32 people once admitted by the host. Only people with a WhatsApp account can create a call link. Guests can use the same essential in-call features like sharing their computer screen to collaborate and review materials, reacting with a thumbs up or heart emoji, or raising their hand to jump in. Later this year we’ll be rolling out new calendar integrations so you can create a WhatsApp call right from your Google or Outlook calendar. Simply install the WhatsApp plugin, connect your account, and add a WhatsApp call link to your invite. Everyone you invite can join with or without a WhatsApp account. Guest calling and calendar integrations are the latest in a series of calling updates we’ve made this year. We believe WhatsApp calling should always work wherever you are and with whoever you need, with the privacy you can count on.

sources.title: ChatGPT can now look at your Chrome tabs to do tasks for you
sources.text: OpenAI has updated its ChatGPT extension to be able to do more browser-based tasks. OpenAI has updated its ChatGPT extension for Chrome , giving it the power to look at your tabs so it can come up with more personalized and useful answers to your queries. The company used to have a browser of its own, but it retired the product on August 9. It did, however, roll out upgrades to the Chrome extension that made ChatGPT a more viable alternative to Gemini in the browser. With these latest updates, ChatGPT can now do even more tasks inside Chrome. If you're in ChatGPT Chat, you can ask the AI assistant to take a look at your open tabs on Chrome to conjure answers that would personally be useful. You can, for instance, ask it to compare couches opened on three different tabs by their dimensions, prices, delivery time and return policy. Meanwhile, if you're using ChatGPT Work, OpenAI's agent designed for complex multi-step tasks, you can ask the assistant to send messages, fill out forms, organize tabs and fill out forms for you. You can ask ChatGPT to fill out a form for your new dentist and then add your schedule to the calendar, for instance. Another example is to get the chatbot to analyze several contractors' terms open in multiple tabs and then draft an email to the provider that fits your needs the most. In addition, ChatGPT in Chrome's sidebar now has access to your whole history, so you can talk to it and give it tasks without having to tab away from what you were doing. You can get the ChatGPT extension, no matter what plan you have. OpenAI says that aside from Chrome, the extension is also compatible with other Chromium-based browsers, including Microsoft Edge, Brave and Opera. Next up: using ChatGPT right within a Chrome tab got a major upgrade – the full power of ChatGPT is now in your browser. Your entire ChatGPT history is right there, and you can ask question in Chat or get things done in Work – side by side while you're on a site. pic.twitter.com/ABiwzLvNnD

stories.title: Open-sourcing SPACE, the sandbox platform behind Computer
stories.summary: Perplexity open-sources SPACE, the sandbox platform behind Computer, to help developers build safer autonomous AI agents

sources.name: Perplexity
sources.title: Open-sourcing SPACE, the sandbox platform behind Computer
sources.text: Perplexity open-sources SPACE, the sandbox platform behind Computer, to help developers build safer autonomous AI agents Since launching Computer in February, Perplexity has been an early pioneer in personal agents. Weâre committed to the hard problems of agent governance, detecting unsafe behaviors and preventing rogue agent activity. In July, we replaced our commercially available sandbox provider with a more robust and resilient in-house solution we named SPACE . SPACE provides high security for advanced agentic systems. In fact, a recent barrage of security testing proved SPACE resilient against network-bypass techniques like those used in the OpenAI/Hugging Face incident. Today, we're open-sourcing SPACE to give developers a foundation for building safer agent systems and contributing to stronger protections across the industry. Developers can access the repository here . Agent governance is an engineering problem , and open source is essential to solving it. When developers have systems they can inspect, adapt, and build on, they find more weaknesses and develop better tools. Open-sourcing SPACE gives developers a production-tested foundation for agent runtimes, with isolation, state recovery, and credential and network controls built in. Sandboxes keep agents secure, letting them access the tools and files they need to complete these tasks, while keeping sensitive information protected. Open-sourcing SPACE gives developers a starting point for the environments where their agents run code and work with files. Teams can see how the SPACE sandbox platform works and build on its implementation. They can also adapt it to their needs rather than recreating the underlying infrastructure. In Computer, SPACE supports isolated code execution, pause and resume, recovery, and session branching. Those capabilities provide the foundation for assistants that could: These examples illustrate how developers could use SPACE's documented isolation and session controls. Platform and security engineers can also review the isolation model and security examples before integrating SPACE into their own systems. When we give agents more room to solve problems, we need clear limits on how they do it. We know that agents pursuing legitimate tasks can still cross security boundaries when they attempt to work around missing files, failed requests, or permission denials. We can put model safeguards into place to reduce the likelihood of unsafe behavior. Adding independent controls in the surrounding system helps contain the damage if those safeguards fail. They limit what an agent can access regardless of what it decides to do. SPACE puts those controls around a separate workspace for agent-generated code and files. We designed it to combine isolation, recovery, and efficient execution. This lets agents perform useful work over long sessions without relying on the model alone to respect security boundaries. Each SPACE sandbox runs inside a small virtual machine with its own operating system, creating an isolation boundary between the agentâs work and the host system. A central control plane coordinates when these workspaces are created, paused, resumed, or removed. SPACE treats the sandbox as untrusted and manages network access and platform-held credentials outside the sandbox. Agents can connect to authorized services without those credentials being stored in their working environment. Frequent file snapshots and checkpoints of the full running environment preserve progress across interruptions. To keep these operations efficient, SPACE stores changes rather than repeatedly copying entire environments. This reduces the work needed to create, restore, or branch a sandbox. Since July, SPACE has powered all Computer sessions and has handled millions of sandbox creations per day. In a comparison on the same production traffic, sandbox creation was three to five times faster than with our previous provider. We also tested SPACE against agents deliberately trying to breach its boundaries. Our published security evaluation found no escape from the virtual machine to the host in 108 attempts, but some found ways around network restrictions. We fixed those weaknesses, and neither identified attack method succeeded in follow-up testing. We also disclosed related weaknesses we found in other sandbox platforms to their vendors, extending that work beyond our own infrastructure. SPACE is part of a broader effort to strengthen the systems people rely on as AI takes on more work. Through the Secure Intelligence Institute , we conduct security research and collaborate with the wider community, translating findings into practical defenses. We believe open-sourcing security tools gives developers more ways to test defenses, find weaknesses, and build safer AI systems. We've shared tools that address different parts of that work: Making these tools available lets other teams inspect our work, adapt it to their needs, and contribute improvements. With SPACE, we're extending that approach to the environments where agents execute code and work with files. Akamai has tested and launched SPACE on its cloud platform and is working with Perplexity to bring it to its customers. Crusoe is also partnering with Perplexity to add SPACE to its Managed AI Services portfolio. CoreWeave has published setup guidance for developers who want to deploy SPACE for evaluation on CKS . Developers can start with the SPACEâs setup instructions and security guidance to deploy it for their own agent systems. The repository and documentation define the supported configurations and included components.

sources.title: Perplexity AI open-sources its secure AI agent sandbox SPACE
sources.text: The artificial intelligence search engine startup Perplexity AI Inc. is shifting its focus to AI agent security in the wake of several high-profile incidents that saw autonomous systems escape from secure environments and go on to wreak havoc on third-party websites. The company has developed an AI sandbox specifically for isolating AI agents called SPACE , and it’s being made open source from today, which means every developer can use the tool to secure their own systems. SPACE is already being deployed by partners including CoreWeave Inc., Akamai Technologies Inc. and Crusoe Inc., which all offer cloud-hosted infrastructure platforms for AI systems. AI sandboxes are the main barrier that prevents AI agents from causing problems like leaking sensitive data or going off and hacking other systems. They’re secure, isolated virtual environments where autonomous agents can run third-party software, browse the internet and execute tasks without risking the security of the host computer, the broader corporate network or underlying data center. By giving each AI agent its own walled-off computer in the cloud, if it makes a mistake, runs a destructive command or is manipulated by adversarial prompts, the damage it does will be contained within that environment. The only problem with AI sandboxes is their security isn’t always foolproof. In fact, there have been several incidents of cunning AI agents managing to find a way to escape from their confines and make trouble elsewhere. One of the most notable involved AI agents being tested by OpenAI Group PBC, which escaped from a sandbox and went on to hack into the model hosting platform Hugging Face. OpenAI’s agents have also hacked websites operated by the U.S. and Australian governments. Most frontier model labs have been focused more on “model alignment,” which involves training AI systems to behave themselves and not look for loopholes in their guardrails, but Perplexity engineer Zibi Braniecki told Semafor his company has instead concentrated on making those guardrails tougher and more reliable. Perplexity developed SPACE to safeguard its Portable Computer agents , which are marketed to its customers as locally-hosted AI agents that can perform tasks on their behalf. They’re designed to do things like developing web applications , research products, buy things online, book hotels and so on. With Perplexity’s Computer agents, SPACE provides safety features such as isolated code execution, pause and resume, recovery and session branching. Agents run within a small virtual machine that has its own operating system, isolating them from the host computer. There’s a user-controlled control plane for creating, running, pausing and deleting these VMs. SPACE ensures that these sandboxes are always treated as “untrusted,” and manages their network access and platform credentials outside of the sandbox, enabling agents to connect to authorized services without that sensitive information ever being made available to them within their environment. It also takes frequent file snapshots and checkpoints of the running environment to preserve progress and ensure it can revert back if any problems occur. So far, though, there hasn’t been any need to do anything like that, for SPACE seems to be bulletproof. Braniecki told Semafar that his team tested nine frontier models in SPACE environments and ordered them specifically to try and break out of their sandbox. In 118 attempts, none of them succeeded, though some did manage to find their way around the network restrictions. However, Perplexity has now fixed those weaknesses, and none of the models were able to do it again in follow-up testing. To compare SPACE’s performance, Perplexity performed the same tests using other, proprietary sandboxes, and said the agents found a way to escape from several of them. Braniecki said the open-source nature of SPACE is key to securing AI agents, because it will enable companies to work together to build the tough guardrails they need. It’s similar to what happened during the early days of web browsers, he said, where the developer community collaborated on the security systems needed to enable secure browning and online commerce. Perplexity isn’t the only company pursuing an open-source approach to AI agent sandboxes. One alternative is Nvidia Corp.’s OpenShell project, which was released last month as part of a broader Open Agent Safety Platform . So far, there have been no reported escapes from OpenShell. Perplexity is not new to open-source security. Besides SPACE, it has also developed open source innovations such as BrowseSafe , which is used to detect malicious instructions hidden in web pages; Numbat , a tool for investigating dangerous agent behaviors; and Bumblebee , which is a scanner that’s used to detect risky AI tool configurations. stories.title: AWS, Anthropic race to deploy army of specialized engineers key to proving AI spending will pay off
stories.summary: AWS, Anthropic, OpenAI and Google are racing to build forward deployed engineering teams as companies seek returns on their AI investments.

sources.name: CNBC Technology
sources.title: AWS, Anthropic race to deploy army of specialized engineers key to proving AI spending will pay off
sources.text: After spending billions building artificial intelligence , Big Tech is now spending heavily to build the human workforce needed to prove the investments are paying off. Companies are scrambling to find specialized AI engineers who can put the technology to work inside businesses. These specialists — called forward deployed engineers, or FDEs — combine advanced AI and software expertise with an understanding of how corporations operate. They could be the key humans in the loop required to turn powerful large language models into enterprise systems that can deliver measurable business results . Market concerns that the economics of the AI boom are not sustainable have intensified this week with many top AI-themed and memory-themed stocks from Dell to CoreWeave, AMD and Micron suffering significant short-term losses. Amazon Web Services has committed $1 billion to a forward-deployed engineering initiative. OpenAI has launched a deployment business backed by more than $4 billion in initial investment. Anthropic is putting $100 million into a program to train 10,000 forward-deployed engineers by the end of 2027. And Accenture and Google Cloud are building a 1,000-person forward-deployed engineering workforce. "The Street is starting to become impatient with these billions of companies who are spending on AI without getting any business outcomes," said Jeff Christian, founder of executive search firm Christian & Timbers. Working directly with customers, FDEs navigate existing technology systems, security requirements, and organizational obstacles to turn promising AI experiments into applications companies can actually use. At Caylent, an AWS consulting partner that embeds FDEs with customers, CEO Val Henderson said the role requires more than technical expertise. "The hardest thing to teach is the customer EQ, without question," she said, adding that engineers also need to understand customers and businesses, navigate organizational dynamics, and exercise judgment when projects encounter unexpected problems. Experienced talent is scarce, and developing that expertise can't happen overnight in a labor market race that recent hiring numbers suggest is accelerating. U.S. job postings for FDEs surged from fewer than 200 in 2023 to approximately 1,200 in 2025 and more than 7,300 in the first nine months of 2026, according to data from labor market analytics firm Lightcast . Median advertised salaries reached $195,456 during that period, up 40% from 2023 and more than three times the median advertised salary across all U.S. job postings. The competition extends well beyond the companies developing AI models. Consulting firms are among the biggest recruiters, reflecting demand for engineers who can help corporate clients implement the technology. Lightcast counted 872 unique FDE job postings from Deloitte and 688 from Accenture during the first nine months of 2026, followed by Google with 499 and KPMG with 447. The figures represent advertised positions, not completed hires. "Demand for forward deployed engineers is rising fast, and growing wages suggest employers are competing for a limited pool of talent," said Elena Magrini, head of global research at Lightcast. But the data also points to a potential solution. "FDE is not an entirely new role. It shares roughly half of its skills with software engineering, creating an opportunity to tap into a much broader talent pool," said Magrini. Technology companies and their corporate clients are investing in multiple ways to develop deployment expertise. AWS is building its own FDE organization, drawing on experienced engineers within Amazon and AWS while also recruiting externally. The company is starting with hundreds of engineers, according to Asa Kalavade, vice president of forward-deployed engineering at AWS. "We are investing $1 billion now because customers need this hands-on help turning their AI investments into results at speed," Kalavade said. OpenAI is pursuing a broader enterprise deployment strategy, backed by the $4 billion in initial investment and an agreement earlier this year to acquire Tomoro , an applied AI consulting and engineering firm expected to bring approximately 150 experienced FDEs and deployment specialists into the operation. Anthropic is taking a different approach, training engineers already employed by its customers and partners. Through its Claude Frontier Academy, the company aims to train 10,000 FDEs by the end of 2027. Its first residency cohorts include engineers from Accenture, Bain, Capgemini, Commonwealth Bank of Australia, Deloitte, McKinsey, Morgan Stanley, and Novo Nordisk. "The AI skills gap affects every customer and every partner, so it is a market problem, and Anthropic is committed to helping close it," said Steve Corfield, Anthropic's global head of business development and partnerships. Accenture and Google Cloud , meanwhile, are building a 1,000-person FDE workforce, relying partly on retraining experienced software engineers for customer-facing AI deployment work. "The reality is that experienced FDEs cannot simply be recruited at the scale clients need," said Ram Ramalingam, Accenture's FDE and software and platform engineering lead. Depending on their backgrounds, the company's FDE training and onboarding can take 30 to 90 days, Ramalingam said. He added that participants already have substantial software engineering experience; the program is designed to add specialized deployment capabilities rather than train beginners. AWS also sees an opportunity to develop expertise inside customer organizations. Kalavade said many businesses already employ capable engineers but need help learning how to move AI projects into production. AWS's FDEs work alongside those teams so customers can eventually maintain and expand the systems themselves. The challenge goes beyond technical expertise, said Corfield. sources.title: Thousands of specialized engineers deployed by AWS, Anthropic to prove AI is worth the investment
sources.text: US tech giants are now spending billions of dollars deploying specialist engineers to help their customers realize the benefits of AI, with AWS, Anthropic, OpenAI and Google all recently announcing expansions to their forward-deployed engineer (FDE) programs. We've already surpassed the point that model capabilities were the limit – now, companies are struggling with legacy infrastructure and identifying real-world use cases, so AI developers are getting involved to help them out. As part of the ongoing shift in how AI is being sold, those developers are no longer just selling their AI to customers – they're also taking responsibility over its deployment. Already, we've seen OpenAI backing its FDE business with a massive $4 billion investment and AWS footing a $1 billion bill for FDEs, while Anthropic shared plans to train 10,000 specialist engineers by the end of 2027. Lightcast research even highlights the extensive growth in FDE job roles, with around 200 FDE job ads shared in the US in 2023 and a similar number in 2024. By 2025, this had increased 6x to around 1,200 advertised positions, yet in the first nine months of 2026 the report found 7,300 roles, another 6x increase year-over-year. "As businesses move from developing AI technology to applying it, they need professionals who can bridge the gap between technical products and operational problems," the report explains. Interestingly, three of the four top companies advertising roles were consultancies (Deloitte, Accenture and KPMG), with just one of them being a tech firm (Google). Consultancies are positioning themselves as a key part of the chain, and Anthropic's recent announcement to support engineer roles within third-party consultancies aligns with this emerging trend. sources.name: Canaltech
sources.title: Meta libera os pesos do Muse Spark Open para rodar em Macs
sources.text: A Meta liberou os pesos do Muse Spark Open , modelo de inteligência artificial focado em programação e tarefas autônomas executadas por agentes de IA. A novidade está disponível para download e acesso por API, Os desenvolvedores interessados podem executar o sistema localmente com dois computadores Mac Studio equipados com chips Apple M5 Ultra. O Muse Spark Open tem 816 bilhões de parâmetros , valores numéricos que ajudam a IA a identificar padrões e gerar respostas. Desse total, 42 bilhões são ativados durante o processamento de cada tarefa. O modelo também tem uma janela de contexto de 1 milhão de tokens , que define a quantidade de informações que consegue considerar em uma interação. A arquitetura multimodal foi desenvolvida para lidar com tarefas complexas de engenharia de software, raciocínio em várias etapas e fluxos de trabalho prolongados. A execução local em Macs utiliza a biblioteca MLX e a memória unificada dos chips M5 Ultra. Cada Mac Studio pode ter até 512 GB de memória compartilhada entre o processador e a GPU. Como o Muse Spark Open precisa de cerca de 1 TB de memória para carregar todos os seus parâmetros, são necessários dois computadores trabalhando em conjunto . Nessa configuração, as máquinas somam até 1 TB de memória e alcançam uma largura de banda de 1,2 TB/s. Os pesos do modelo também estão disponíveis para download em plataformas , como Hugging Face, Amazon SageMaker AI, Google Cloud Model Garden e Microsoft Foundry Models. A Meta demonstrou o modelo em tarefas autônomas com o Muse Code , ferramenta de programação baseada no Muse Spark Open. Em um dos testes, o sistema modificou o aplicativo de código aberto Ice Cubes, cliente da rede social Mastodon para iOS, com correções de bugs, criação de recursos e compilação completa do projeto. Em outra demonstração, o modelo controlou o DaVinci Resolve para analisar vídeos quadro a quadro , selecionar os melhores trechos e ajustar o enquadramento para o formato vertical. Os exemplos mostram aplicações do sistema em atividades que envolvem diferentes etapas de execução, da análise inicial à conclusão da tarefa. O modelo também é compatível com ferramentas de inferência, como SGLang, vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, Hugging Face Transformers, llama.cpp e Unsloth, além de oferecer otimizações para hardware da AMD, Apple, Intel e NVIDIA. Além disso, a licença Muse Model License estabelece condições específicas de uso comercial e oferece acesso gratuito para a maioria dos desenvolvedores. Para personalizar o modelo, é possível utilizar PyTorch com TorchTitan, enquanto a execução em Macs com Apple Silicon depende da biblioteca MLX. A Meta afirma que o Muse Spark Open passou por um processo de pós-treinamento com foco em segurança e foi avaliado segundo os critérios do Meta Superintelligence Scaling Framework antes da publicação dos pesos. Se você gostou do conteúdo, talvez também se interesse por conferir “ Por que a China está dando de graça suas IAs mais avançadas? ”.

sources.title: OCP Global Summit: Amid Ecosystem Adoption, NVIDIA Opens Vera Rubin Architecture to Help Scale AI Factories Worldwide
sources.text: As AI factories grow from megawatts to gigawatts, building them takes more than advanced computing. Open standards are helping the industry scale AI infrastructure faster, more efficiently and more reliably. At the Open Compute Project (OCP) Global Summit, taking place in the San Jose McEnery Convention Center, NVIDIA announced new partnerships and contributions aimed at creating a common foundation for next-generation AI infrastructure. NVIDIA contributed key NVIDIA Vera Rubin rack and compute tray designs to OCP through the open NVIDIA MGX architecture, giving system builders a common foundation for developing next-generation AI factory infrastructure. Together, these efforts span the AI factory itself, the utility grid that powers it and the rack-scale architecture at the heart of modern accelerated computing. At the OCP event, NVIDIA and partners made a handful of announcements: Before a packed audience, Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA, discussed how open infrastructure is becoming a critical ingredient for scaling AI factories worldwide. The news at OCP spotlights how NVIDIA’s extreme codesign combined with open standards is accelerating deployment, improving power efficiency and driving tokens-per-watt performance. NVIDIA joined industry leaders in contributing to the third-generation MGX AI data center reference design through OCP’s Open DC Initiative. Combined with open liquid-cooling technologies such as MQD and MQDB, the effort helps turn proven AI factory designs into industry standards that others can adopt, manufacture and scale. For NVIDIA Vera Rubin AI factories, the updated MGX 1.2 specification extends the open architecture for AI factories with rack-scale blind-mate liquid cooling, interoperable rack-scale interconnect infrastructure and a liquid-cooled 5,000A busbar designed for higher-power AI systems. It also adds native 19-inch equipment support and higher-density rack designs. MGX 1.2 further expands modularity with configurable I/O bays, fanless liquid-cooled compute trays, standardized power and cooling interfaces, and a common infrastructure that helps ecosystem partners build interoperable accelerated computing platforms. It improves assembly, test and service times to streamline manufacturing and field service to enable faster and more efficient infrastructure buildout. The architecture supports rack deployments up to 250kW while simplifying serviceability, deployment and infrastructure reuse. The Vera CPU rack design specification extends the NVIDIA MGX open architecture beyond accelerated computing, providing a purpose-built platform for the growing agentic AI era. While Vera Rubin NVL72 serves as the foundation for large-scale training and inference, the NVIDIA Vera CPU rack is designed to support tool calling, orchestration and sandboxed execution, helping AI agents interact with applications, data and services in real time. Built on the third-generation NVIDIA MGX rack architecture, the Vera CPU rack shares the same rack-scale design principles that unite compute, networking, power and cooling into a common modular platform. This approach enables partners to deploy specialized infrastructure while benefiting from a shared ecosystem, simplified integration and a consistent foundation for next-generation AI factories. NVIDIA DSX AI factory platform applies extreme codesign to unify computing, networking, power, cooling, facilities and software, helping AI factories operate as a single optimized system, maximizing AI output within available infrastructure constraints. At the center of this unified system is DSX OS, the open operating layer that turns the DSX architecture into coordinated, repeatable operations at scale. At OCP, NVIDIA expanded DSX OS with open source components for configuring networks, validating clusters, managing racks and provisioning bare metal: Developed from NVIDIA’s experience running NVIDIA DGX Cloud, these open source components enable cloud providers and software partners to integrate AI factory capabilities directly into their multi-tenant platforms. Developers can visit the DSX AI Factory Github page to explore and contribute to both the new and existing open source software components from NVIDIA DSX AI Factory platform. For AI infrastructure to scale globally, it needs more than advanced hardware — it needs a common foundation that the entire industry can build on. At OCP, NVIDIA joined AMD, Google and Meta t o publish a new open specification that establishes that foundation. The Open Data Center Specification v0.7 defines a unified blueprint for next-generation AI factory facility design — from power architecture to cooling infrastructure to physical layout. The OCP Grid Resilience Specification , published by Google , Meta, Microsoft and NVIDIA, establishes how large-scale AI infrastructure should behave during utility grid disturbances: staying connected, responding automatically and restoring to near-full load within less than two seconds. With these standards now open, manufacturers around the world have a common target to build for. Equipment makers, colocation providers and data center operators can begin designing, fabricating and delivering the infrastructure layer that powers AI factories under construction globally — without waiting for proprietary specifications from individual customers. Being NVIDIA DSX reference design -compatible, these specifications provide a validated, deployable implementation of both specs, from facility layout and power architecture to the software that monitors and responds to grid signals in real time. For operators building Vera Rubin AI factories, there’s now a straight line from open community standard to a running system. As AI factories grow larger and more powerful, one challenge looms over them all: delivering enough power to the accelerated computing systems driving the next generation of AI.
